⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

This page traces how telemetry moves through the platform: what produces metrics and logs, what collects and stores them, and where the dashboards live. It is wiring only — what the log and audit content means, and the commands to read it, belong to the operate guides linked at the end.

The pipeline at a glance

Everything observability-related lives in the monitoring namespace (plus linkerd-viz for the mesh dashboard) and follows one shape: Alloy ships container logs to Loki, Prometheus scrapes metrics and fires alerts at Alertmanager, and Grafana sits on top of all three as the single dashboard surface. blocks.html:
Operators first, instances second

The observability stack is the clearest concrete example of the platform's phased apply model (see Deployment model). It is deployed in two separated steps:

  • **infra-phase1** installs the controllers and their CRDs, but no observability workloads: k8s/prometheus-operator/ (the stripped-down CRD bundle plus the operator's reference RBAC and Deployment manifests, pinned to the upstream v0.91.0 release) and k8s/grafana-operator/ (the v5.22.2 cluster-scoped release bundle).
  • The **monitoring** phase (k8s/main/<env>/monitoring/kustomization.yaml) then applies the actual instances: monitoring-namespace, monitoring-loki, monitoring-alloy, monitoring-kube-state-metrics, monitoring-prometheus, monitoring-grafana, and linkerd-viz.

The split exists because a Prometheus or Grafana CR can only be applied once its CRD is registered, and only does anything once its operator is running. The taskfile applies phases strictly in order, so by the time the monitoring phase renders, both operators are watching. The Prometheus, Alertmanager and Grafana pods you see running are not in any kustomization — the operators reconcile them into existence from the CRs:

Not everything in the monitoring phase is operator-managed: Loki and linkerd-viz are Helm charts rendered by kustomize (--enable-helm), Alloy is plain manifests, and kube-state-metrics is the upstream standard manifest set pinned to the release-2.19 branch.

Metrics

The Prometheus CR (name prometheus, namespace monitoring) stamps every exported series with an external label and selects its scrape configuration by label:

apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: Prometheus
metadata:
  name: prometheus
spec:
  externalLabels:
    cluster: opendefence
  serviceMonitorSelector:
    matchLabels:
      monitoring: prometheus
  scrapeConfigSelector:
    matchLabels:
      monitoring: prometheus
  ruleSelector:
    matchLabels:
      monitoring: prometheus
  alerting:
    alertmanagers:
    - namespace: monitoring
      name: alertmanager-main
      port: web

Anything that wants to be scraped must ship a ServiceMonitor or ScrapeConfig labeled monitoring: prometheus; nothing is discovered without it. The set defined in k8s/monitoring-prometheus/base/resources/:

Target Defined as What it provides
node-exporter (DaemonSet, quay.io/prometheus/node-exporter:v1.11.1, :9100) ServiceMonitor Host-level CPU, memory, disk, network per node
kube-state-metrics ServiceMonitor Kubernetes object state (deployments, pods, jobs…)
kubelet (/metrics, /metrics/cadvisor, /metrics/resource) ServiceMonitor Node runtime + per-container resource usage
Kubernetes API server, CoreDNS ServiceMonitors Control-plane health
Prometheus itself ServiceMonitor Self-monitoring
Linkerd control plane + data-plane proxies ScrapeConfigs Mesh golden metrics (see below)

Note what is not on the list: the product workloads. There are no application-level ServiceMonitors in the repo — request metrics for meshed services (rmapi, Keycloak, the product integration APIs) come from their Linkerd proxy sidecars, and battlelog, which is not meshed, is not scraped at all. Extending coverage means adding a ServiceMonitor labeled monitoring: prometheus.

Alerting rules live in the PrometheusRule named cluster-alerts: node alerts (NodeNotReady, HighNodeMemoryUsage, HighNodeCPUUsage), pod alerts (PodCrashLooping, PodStuckPending, PodNotReady) and JobFailed. Fired alerts go to the Alertmanager CR main (1 replica), addressed as alertmanager-main on port web (:9093); its configuration comes from the Secret alertmanager-main.

Two rough edges to state plainly:

  • The Alertmanager route delivers to a single default receiver whose webhook_configs list is empty. Alerts fire, group, and are visible in Alertmanager and Grafana — but nothing is notified anywhere until an operator configures a real receiver.
  • The Prometheus CR requests no persistent storage: the TSDB lives on the pod's ephemeral volume, so metrics history is lost when the pod restarts, and the operator's default retention (24h) applies. Loki keeps logs for 30 days; Prometheus keeps metrics for one.

Logs

Log collection is deliberately simple. Alloy (grafana/alloy:v1.16.1) runs as a single-replica Deployment opendefence-alloy in monitoring — not a per-node DaemonSet. It discovers pods through the Kubernetes API and reads their output through the pods/log API (its ClusterRole grants get/list/watch on namespaces, pods, pods/log), so log traffic flows through the kubelet/API server rather than host file mounts. The pipeline in config.alloy relabels each stream with namespace, pod, container, app and job (= namespace/container), adds the static label cluster=opendefence, and pushes to the chart's gateway Service at http://opendefence-loki-gateway.monitoring.svc.cluster.local/loki/api/v1/push.

Loki is deployed from Helm chart 17.1.0 (release opendefence-loki) in its smallest possible shape:

deploymentMode: Monolithic
minio:
  enabled: false
singleBinary:
  replicas: 1
  persistence:
    size: 10Gi
table_manager:
  retention_deletes_enabled: true
  retention_period: 30d

All microservice components (read/write/backend, ingester, querier, compactor, …) are explicitly disabled; storage is filesystem with TSDB schema v13, replication_factor: 1, and auth_enabled: false (single tenant).

The tradeoff is stated plainly: this is a single-node log store with no object storage. It fits the platform's single-node deployable-unit target and avoids an S3/MinIO dependency, but the entire log history lives on one 10Gi PVC — lose that volume (or its node) and the logs are gone, there are no backups (consistent with the platform-wide posture, see Data & secrets), and there is no horizontal scaling path without re-architecting onto object storage. Retention is a hard 30 days.

Dashboards

Grafana is instantiated by the grafana-operator from the Grafana CR named grafana, which the operator reconciles into a Grafana Deployment and the grafana-service Service (:3000). The default admin Secret is disabled; the admin user is admin and the password comes from the Secret grafana-admin-password, generated in-cluster by an External Secrets Operator Password generator with refreshInterval: "0" — generated once at install, never rotated automatically, never chosen by a human (the same pattern as every other platform secret).

Datasources are declared as GrafanaDatasource CRs, matched to the instance via instanceSelector label dashboards: grafana:

Datasource URL
Loki http://opendefence-loki-gateway.monitoring.svc.cluster.local
Prometheus http://prometheus-operated.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090
Alertmanager http://alertmanager-main.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9093

Dashboards are code, too: GrafanaDashboard CRs ship a Loki-backed pod-logs-dashboard plus six Prometheus dashboards (k8s-system-api-server, k8s-system-coredns, k8s-views-global, k8s-views-namespaces, k8s-views-nodes, k8s-views-pods).

Exposure: a Traefik IngressRoute on the websecure entrypoint routes grafana.<domain> (locally also grafana.localhost) to grafana-service:3000. The server certificate comes from the grafana-tls Secret — issued by the internal intermediate-ca-issuer in the local overlay and by letsencrypt-http01-production in cloud. Unlike the product routes, the Grafana route sets no TLSOption and no callsign middleware chain — there is no client-certificate (mTLS) requirement; the only gate is Grafana's own login with the generated admin password. See Ingress & network edge for how this compares to the mTLS-guarded hosts.

Mesh telemetry

linkerd-viz (Helm chart 30.12.11, namespace linkerd-viz, itself meshed) normally ships its own bundled Prometheus. The platform disables that and points it at the cluster instance instead:

valuesInline:
  prometheusUrl: http://prometheus-operated.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090
  prometheus:
    enabled: false

The scrape jobs the bundled Prometheus would have run are ported into three ScrapeConfig CRs in k8s/monitoring-prometheus/base/resources/linkerd-scrapeconfigs.yaml (adapted from Linkerd's external-Prometheus reference config, labeled monitoring: prometheus so the Prometheus CR picks them up): linkerd-controller (control-plane and viz pods), linkerd-proxy (cluster-wide, every meshed pod's sidecar), and linkerd-service-mirror (a no-op on a single-cluster install, kept for parity). The result is one Prometheus for everything: the linkerd-viz dashboard and CLI read per-route success rates and latencies from the same store that holds node and cluster metrics. How the mesh itself is wired — identity, injection, which workloads are meshed — is covered in Service mesh (Linkerd).

Where to go next

This page stops at the plumbing. What the collected logs actually contain — audit-log semantics, the log categories worth watching, and the concrete commands to query them — is documented in Audit logging & observability. Routine monitoring work — what to check daily, disk-pressure watchpoints, getting into Grafana and using the shipped dashboards — is in Day-2 operations (Kubernetes).
